chapter: Tiger Rag and Mopah Blues explained
title: Disputing Tiger Rag claims and explaining its sources again
summary: He rejects the Lomax-found claimant and again breaks down Tiger Rag, with Howard Jacobs's Newsweek visit.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, there we go again. As much has been said about the Tiger Rag, Alan Lomax discovered a man, well, called Jelero Martin. A man who's never been honored or given credit for anything. That he's done anything. Maybe he played good jazz, I don't know. But it would have to be after the original Dixieland jazz band, because I never heard him, and I never heard him today. They discovered this man, and he goes in the archers of the United States government somewhere, where they keep this folk music. Set him up two jugs of wine, probably seven needles, that he could use, and he could get his story out right. I would not only want to dispute him and all the rest of them on this Tiger Rag, I'll tell you how this Tiger Rag came about. I was elementary. I didn't know nothing. I was self-taught on the carnet. Where the tunes come in, my inability as a gifted musician, only having a few little ideas about me to put to use the different parts and make a number. I'll tie you on the cuff. Howard Jacobs must have the letter in his possession yet because he showed it to me. And that's how Remmelade, he wrote this story, Jazz Prophet Without Honor in his own hometown. And I explained to him where this tune was composed. I was elementary, that's true. I had no learning on that one. Just like a fake or a gypsy would have to find how to make different things. And I was so on my own that I couldn't read music. I had to find new methods of making new tunes. And that's how these tunes come about. Because every number that I have, I can prove to you the source where it came from. And the idea how it was arrived at. Let's go. Whoa, whoa, whoa. Okay, it's working now. Go ahead. When our first record came out, or before our first record came out, it was called Lyrics Table Blues. Mr. King of the Victor Company thought that the title suggested and asked us to change it to Barnyard Blues. We had the name, the title of the tune changed. It was copyrighted. The man who had his numbers copyrighted was our manager, Max Hart. He copyrighted a number under his name. Also, the copyright owner was under his name. This record was released. And when the Victor Company put it out, it was Lyrics Table Blues. Al C. Nunez, who had been my first client editor in Chicago, he told this Roger Graham that was his tune. They looked it up. And they found that we didn't have the copyright on the Lyrics Table Blues. So, Wood Kelly, Roger Graham, Nunez, and Wilcox. The client player, the cornet player of Brown's Band. They went into Sherman Hotel, and they got some men to take this down in notation. And they published this tune, Lyrics Table Blues. I had taken an injunction against them. And when we went to court, the question wasn't on the Lyrics Table Blues. They said, I rehashed this tune from the Morpah Blues. And the Morpah Blues is supposed to be owned by Lopez. My lawyer didn't know, I didn't know music. I couldn't explain how this thing came about. They said it was the same chord construction. But the lawyer didn't take in mind that this tune that they'd taken off the record was the Lyrics Table Blues. It was the same tune I had played on the record in comparison with the Barnyard Blues. They were bringing in another tune that they had no music to, and said it was the same tune. So, the judge said there's so much lying in the case on both sides that he put the thing in public domain. There was nothing to the tune. And in your two-inch files, you'll find this article of the judges, the witnesses and all. And the witnesses packed. Now, when I play you the Lyrics Table Blues, and I'll play you this other tune, let any musician tell me that they're alike. Now, there's one difference in them. I want to explain to you. The reason I call it the Moaning Blues, because when I got back to New York, Mr. Booker wanted to take it to High Court, because he said that they were not talking on the merits of the Mopah Blues, they were talking on the merits of being similar to the Lyrics Table Blues, which they had copied from the record. And my piece that I had played on the record, and he said, certainly there must have been some comparison. He said it was a miscarriage and a thing.
